reason: The supplied proof is invalid because \(y\) is fixed, whereas Step 3 varies \(Y=y^2\) through all positive squares while retaining the same constant \(C\). The corrected proof preserves the quantifier over \(n\) and obtains infinitely many prime divisors forcing \(x^2-1=0\).
text:
Let \(S\) be the set of odd primes dividing \((ny)^2+1\) for at least one positive integer \(n\). This set is infinite. Indeed, if \(S\) were finite and \(Q=\prod_{q\in S}q\) (with \(Q=1\) if \(S\) were empty), then
\[
(2Qy)^2+1>1
\]
would be odd and hence would have an odd prime divisor \(q\in S\). But \(q\mid Q\), so \((2Qy)^2+1\equiv1\pmod q\), a contradiction.

Fix \(q\in S\), and choose \(a>0\) such that \(q\mid(ay)^2+1\). Then \(q\nmid ay\), and \(-1\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(q\), so \(q\equiv1\pmod4\). The hypothesis also shows \(q\nmid x\). Let
\[
d=\operatorname{ord}_q(x).
\]
For every prime \(r\equiv a\pmod q\), we have \(q\mid(ry)^2+1\); hence the hypothesis with \(n=r\) gives
\[
x^{r-1}=x^{\varphi(r)}\equiv1\pmod q,
\]
so \(d\mid r-1\).

We prove that \(d\mid2\), using Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions. If an odd prime \(\ell\) divided \(d\), the Chinese remainder theorem would give a reduced residue class \(b\pmod{q\ell}\) satisfying
\[
b\equiv a\pmod q,\qquad b\equiv2\pmod\ell.
\]
Dirichlet's theorem supplies a prime \(r\equiv b\pmod{q\ell}\). Then \(d\mid r-1\), but \(\ell\nmid r-1\), contradicting \(\ell\mid d\). Thus \(d\) has no odd prime divisor.

Likewise, choose by the Chinese remainder theorem and Dirichlet's theorem a prime
\[
r\equiv a\pmod q,\qquad r\equiv3\pmod4.
\]
Again \(d\mid r-1\), while \(v_2(r-1)=1\). Therefore \(4\nmid d\). Consequently \(d\mid2\), and hence
\[
x^2\equiv1\pmod q.
\]
Thus every \(q\in S\) divides the fixed integer \(x^2-1\). Since \(S\) is infinite, this is possible only if \(x^2-1=0\). As \(x\) is positive, \(x=1\).
